doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Neighbor bassist and the four records
summary: Learning by ear, he got four records on a neighbor's advice: Miles Davis, Ferguson, Mendez and Butterfield, and his mother's cooking.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Okay. You must have not been a person who was afraid to take a chance, to basically improvise?

No. I didn’t learn by reading music. Because even though I started in the public schools you know that was sort of fundamentally [scats] and but my neighbor was a bass player. My back neighbor where I would climb over the fence and he had a little jazz group that he would rehearse. He was like an engineer at Sperry Gyroscope out on Long Island. He played bass. Genius. He was telling me about how they were working on the gyroscopes that would send the rockets up and stuff. I mean he was great. But my dad said to him, my dad was a tap dancer during the war, overseas. I mean he did everything from being a cook to a tank driver, and he would entertain tap dancing when they were doing some sort of event to keep everybody upbeat. You know? And so what was I saying — so he asked the bass player, in the back, he said, “Hey Bob, you know my son’s been playing trumpet and I think he sounds pretty good, so is there any recordings that I should have, I should get him?” And we didn’t have a lot of money. So he named like four recordings and it was Miles Davis, Maynard Ferguson, Rafael Mendez and Billy Butterfield.

Yep. That’s why I think he, this guy was like I say, he was really organized in his thoughts and his work. So I had these four records, you know the LPs and a changer. And every day after school that’s what I did. I practiced. I did my homework first, always. My schoolwork. And so then I did my trumpet until dinner. I did my homework while my mom was cooking I did it in the kitchen at the table. And she was cooking and I said [sniffs] “Oh what is that, Mom? That smells really good.” And that’s how I learned to cook. I never cooked for many years except by smell when I finally started to cook a lot I just remembered what it smelled like. I said, “I think this is close.” And then, “I think that was too much garlic maybe.” So I would practice with these records at least an hour a day.
